old_options <- options(width = 100)
library(masque)
set.seed(1)

f <- system.file("extdata", "john_alpha.csv", package = "masque")
df <- read.csv(f, stringsAsFactors = TRUE)
plan <- propose_roles(df, mode = "collaborate")
```

## Why

An analyst has the synthetic table and their own code. The data owner
keeps the original and the recipe. This vignette covers what the recipe carries,
how the analyst's finished pipeline is run on the original, and what
happens when the original holds a value the recipe has never seen.

The examples use `mode = "collaborate"`, because the default mode
(`"null"`) keeps no structure beyond the design. The recipe works the same
way in every mode.

## What

The recipe, taken from a `mask()` result with `recipe()`, holds the real
labels, the original column names and the seed. Together with the
synthetic it undoes every alias, so keep it with the original data and never send it with the
synthetic.

Two functions make the round-trip. `apply_recipe()` recodes the original
data into the clone's labels and column names, which is how a data owner
runs an analyst's finished pipeline on it. `unmask()` goes the other way
and turns a result in the clone's labels back into the original ones.
`save_recipe()` and `read_recipe()` write and read a recipe as a single
`.rds` file, and `reveal_maps()` prints the level maps that a redacted `print()`
withholds.

## Example

### What a recipe holds

```{r accessors}
m <- mask(df, plan, mode = "collaborate", seed = 1L)
rec <- recipe(m)
class(rec)
```

A recipe holds:

- `masque_version`, `created_at`, `mode`: provenance.
- `seed`: the seed of the call. With it the same call reproduces the same
  alias maps, so keep it as private as the maps.
- `roles`: each column's role and action, with the original column
  names.
- `conditional`, `ladder`, `conditioning_cols`, `conditioning_used`,
  `conditioning_dropped`, `conditioning_shifted`, `fallback_frac`: what a
  conditional clone asked for, the stratum it got, the columns it dropped
  or carried as shifts, and the share of rows pooled.
- `level_maps`: the per-column original-to-alias maps. This is the sensitive part. Aliases follow one scheme: `trt_001`, `trt_002`, ... for a single
  aliased treatment, factor or numeric (`<col>_trt_001` when several
  treatments are aliased), `<col>_L001` for a categorical
  covariate, `<col>_D001` for a design column, `<col>_I001` for an
  identifier, `<col>_T001` for free text, and `<col>_K001` for a key
  shared across the tables of a set. The numbers have at least three
  digits, more when a column has over 999 levels.
- `column_name_map`: the column-name aliases, when `alias_names` was
  used (otherwise `NULL`).
- `storage_classes`, `factor_meta`: the original column classes, factor
  levels and ordering, for faithful reconstruction.
- `cleaning`: the tidying done before masking (column names made valid
  R names, whitespace trimmed), so `apply_recipe()` re-applies the same
  tidying.
- `conform`: the label merges and type changes `conform_table()` made, so
  `apply_recipe()` replays them on the original.
- `grain`: for each design unit whose columns were synthesised once per
  unit, the columns, the number of units, and whether the clone kept the
  unit or fell back to rows.
- `events`: the linked time-to-event specs and how many final times were
  capped.
- `coords`: one entry per coordinate pair declared to `mask()`'s
  `coords` argument: the jitter method and radius, the site grouping it
  was masked under, and how many sites the grouping produced.
- `allow_unmasked_coords`: `TRUE` only when the caller deliberately
  wrote a real coordinate through unmasked.
- `allow_kept_outcome`: `TRUE` only when the caller allowed a kept outcome
  in a default or collaborate clone.
- `noise`: the draw behind the `noise` action, `"summary"` or
  `"standard"`.
- `plan` and `owner_key`: the plan the clone was made from, resolved on the
  original, and a private key for the data owner's known-truth controls.
  Both are empty when `mask()` was not given a plan.
- `warnings`: the warnings raised while masking, including any HIGH
  audit finding.
- `content_fp` and `integrity_fp`: fingerprints of the original's values
  (two weighted sums per numeric column and a digest of the rest) and of
  its missing-value pattern (a SHA-256 of `is.na(original)`).
  `apply_recipe()` uses them to check it was given the same table. They are
  integrity checks, not privacy guarantees.

A recipe written by an older version has no record for the slots added
since, for example `coords` before 0.10.0 and `allow_unmasked_coords`
before 0.11.0. It still prints, applies and unmasks. The changelog lists
when each slot was added.

It does not hold the copula covariance, the values of any re-simulated or
noise column, or any file paths or usernames.

A recipe built with `coords` records how its coordinates were masked, so
an audit of the recipe does not need the original data back:

```{r coords-account, eval = requireNamespace("maps", quietly = TRUE)}
df_geo <- df
df_geo$lat <- -34.9 + stats::runif(nrow(df_geo), -0.05, 0.05)
df_geo$lon <- 138.6 + stats::runif(nrow(df_geo), -0.05, 0.05)
plan_geo <- propose_roles(df_geo, mode = "collaborate")
plan_geo <- set_role(plan_geo, c("lat", "lon"), action = "keep")

m_geo <- mask(df_geo, plan_geo, mode = "collaborate", seed = 1L,
              coords = list(list(lat = "lat", lon = "lon")))
n_sites_recorded <- recipe(m_geo)@coords[[1]]$n_sites
recipe(m_geo)@coords[[1]][c("method", "min_km", "max_km", "n_sites")]
recipe(m_geo)@allow_unmasked_coords
```

```{r coords-account-skip, eval = !requireNamespace("maps", quietly = TRUE), echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat("maps is not installed on this build, so the coordinate-account demo",
    "is skipped.\n")
n_sites_recorded <- NA_integer_
```

Each plot here has its own coordinate, so each plot is a site and
`n_sites` equals the number of plots. Rows that share a coordinate would
share one displacement (see `jitter_coordinates()`).

### Printing is redacted

The print method shows the role and action table with a marker for which
columns hold a level map (`*` mapped, `=` not), but never the vocabularies
themselves:

```{r print-redacted}
rec
```

The same holds for `format()`, `str()` and knitr output of a recipe and of
a `masque` object, so the seed and the maps do not end up in a log or a
rendered report by accident. Anyone holding the recipe can print the maps with an explicit call, which
shows a warning first. Its output, 24 genotype labels, is left out here:

```{r reveal, message = FALSE}
reveal_maps(rec)
```

### The round-trip

The usual pattern is to fit on the synthetic, recode the original with
`apply_recipe()`, and predict on it:

```{r roundtrip-pipeline}
# Analyst trains on the synthetic clone.
fit <- lm(yield ~ gen, data = synthetic(m))

# The data owner runs the same pipeline on the real data.
orig_in_synth_space <- apply_recipe(df, rec)
preds <- predict(fit, newdata = orig_in_synth_space)
preds_match_nrow <- length(preds) == nrow(df)
preds_match_nrow
```

`unmask()` recovers the original labels:

```{r roundtrip-labels}
fwd <- apply_recipe(df, rec)
back <- unmask(fwd, rec)
labels_recovered <- identical(as.character(back$gen), as.character(df$gen))
labels_recovered
```

Columns whose action is `keep`, re-simulated numeric columns and numeric
predictions pass through both functions unchanged. A numeric treatment
that was aliased is mapped both ways, and `unmask()` returns its exact
original values. `apply_recipe()` returns an aliased factor with the
clone's levels in the clone's order, so a model fitted on
the translated original has the same reference level as on the clone.

### Fail-closed translation

If the data drifts, for example a new treatment level the recipe has
never seen, `apply_recipe()` stops with an error. Any change to the values
also fails the integrity check, which runs first, so the example turns
that check off to reach the label check:

```{r fail-closed, error = TRUE}
drifted <- df
levels(drifted$gen) <- c(levels(df$gen), "BRAND_NEW")
drifted$gen[1] <- "BRAND_NEW"
apply_recipe(drifted, rec, check_integrity = FALSE)
```

The message names the column (`gen`) and the value (`"BRAND_NEW"`). Either
remove the drifted rows before running the pipeline, or mask the data
that contains the new value again. Masking again makes a new recipe and a new
synthetic, and the analyst needs the new synthetic in place of the old
one.

### Saving the recipe

`save_recipe()` writes a single small `.rds`, to be stored next to the
original at the same security class. The path must end in `.rds`.
`read_recipe()` validates the file and notes a version mismatch without
raising an error.

```{r save}
tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
save_recipe(rec, tmp)
rec2 <- read_recipe(tmp)
fingerprint_survives_roundtrip <- identical(
  rec@integrity_fp, rec2@integrity_fp
)
fingerprint_survives_roundtrip
```

### Multi-table bundles

A `mask_set()` result carries a recipe *bundle*: one recipe per table
plus the shared cross-table link maps. The same `apply_recipe()` and
`unmask()` verbs dispatch on it, operating table by table over a named
list. `year` is made a factor before masking so that collaborate mode can
alias it (see *Getting started with masque*):

```{r set-bundle}
set_dir <- system.file("extdata", "met_set", package = "masque")
originals <- read_set(set_dir)
originals$agronomy[, year := factor(year)]
ms <- mask_set(originals, mode = "collaborate", seed = 1L, quiet = TRUE)
fwd_set <- apply_recipe(originals, recipe(ms))
names(fwd_set)
```

`save_recipe()` and `read_recipe()` keep a bundle as one file, and
`reveal_maps(recipe(ms), table = "quality")` reveals the maps of the named
table only.

Because the shared keys were aliased consistently at masking time, the
recoded tables join on the same keys the synthetic tables do.

### Figure: original against synthetic yield

The checks above are about labels. The figure shows the numeric column the
analyst works with: the original yield against the synthetic yield.

```{r fig-overlay, eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE), fig.cap = "Density of yield, original trial against the synthetic clone. The two distributions overlap closely because collaborate mode draws each re-simulated numeric column from its own marginal distribution.", fig.alt = "Two overlapping density curves of yield, original and synthetic, with nearly the same shape."}
synth_tbl <- synthetic(m)
overlay_df <- rbind(
  data.frame(value = df$yield, table = "original"),
  data.frame(value = synth_tbl$yield, table = "synthetic")
)
ggplot2::ggplot(overlay_df, ggplot2::aes(x = value, fill = table)) +
  ggplot2::geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_viridis_d(name = "table") +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "yield (t/ha)", y = "density"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()
```

```{r fig-overlay-skip, eval = !requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE), echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat("ggplot2 is not installed on this build, so the marginal-overlay",
    "figure is skipped.\n")
```

## Results

All three round-trip checks pass: one prediction per original row, the
original genotype labels recovered, and the same integrity fingerprint
after the recipe is saved and read back. A value the recipe has never seen
stops the translation where the data drifted.

The two yield densities overlap closely, so the marginal distribution is
kept. That says nothing about whether a treatment effect or a non-linear
relationship between columns is kept. *Confidentiality and the threat
model* covers both.

With the recipe, the data owner can run the analyst's finished pipeline
on the real data without changing it.

## Limits

This vignette uses one recipe built from one clean public trial, with one
planted drift. By default `apply_recipe()` accepts only the table the
recipe was built from. With `check_integrity = FALSE` it runs on updated
data, and labels added since masking are still refused. The round-trip
functions invert only what the recipe recorded. Numeric columns pass
through unchanged, so `unmask()` cannot undo a numeric transformation a
pipeline made, and a recipe cannot repair a join that was broken before
masking. The leakage audit, the conditional clone
and the coordinate controls are covered in *Confidentiality and the threat
model*.

## What to read next

*Getting started with masque* is the data owner's side of this same handover: building and reviewing the masking plan that produces the recipe
this vignette reads. *Confidentiality and the threat model* sets out what
the recipe and the synthetic together do and do not protect, including the
leakage audit and the conditional clone that mimics a treatment effect.

## Reproduce

`set.seed(1)` is set once for the document, and every `mask()` or
`mask_set()` call passes `seed = 1L`, so each is reproducible on its own.
Package versions follow.

sessionInfo()
```
